methods.label: Compare Alice's and Ellen's possible pairs
methods.explanation:
All ten throws hit different values, so no value can occur in two friends' pairs. The two largest totals are useful because they allow very few pairs of distinct numbers from \(1\) through \(10\).

Alice's total of \(16\) can only be
\[
6+10\quad\text{or}\quad7+9.
\]
A smaller value than \(6\) would need a partner greater than \(10\), and \(8+8\) repeats a value. Ellen's total of \(17\) can only be
\[
7+10\quad\text{or}\quad8+9.
\]
If Alice used \(7\) and \(9\), Ellen's first possible pair would repeat \(7\), and her second would repeat \(9\). Therefore Alice must use \(6\) and \(10\).

This is compatible with all the other totals: Ben can use \(1,3\), Cindy \(2,5\), Dave \(4,7\), and Ellen \(8,9\). Hence Alice hits the \(6\)-point region, choice A.
